text: Every threat feed describes the same indicator differently. A STIX/TAXII feed wraps an IP inside a pattern string. A CSV export just has a column called ip. A JSON feed buries it three levels deep. If your lookup and scoring code has to understand every one of those shapes directly, every new feed you add means new code and a growing pile of edge cases — so this lesson builds a normalization layer instead, one function per feed format, so everything downstream only ever has to understand one shape.

TAXII 2.1 is the transport, STIX 2.1 is the data format riding on top of it, and the taxii2-client and stix2 libraries handle both. You connect to a server, grab the collection you want, and query it for objects of type indicator — the library deals with paging and authentication, so you start from a list of STIX Indicator objects, each with a pattern string, a confidence score, and a valid_from timestamp.

Not every feed bothers with STIX. Plenty of internal or open-source feeds just publish CSV or JSON over HTTP, so you pull those with requests.get and parse rows with csv.DictReader. Whatever came in, the pipeline is the same three steps: pull the raw feed in whatever shape it arrives, run it through a normalize function for that specific format, then dedupe across every feed you pulled.

That normalize function's whole job is producing one shared dataclass — ioc_type, value, source, confidence, first_seen, and tags — no matter whether the input was a STIX pattern string or a CSV row. Once an indicator is a NormalizedIOC, every later step in this chapter, the SIEM lookups, the scoring pass, and the push back into detection rules, only ever has to know this one schema.

One more step before this is usable: dedupe. The same IP shows up across multiple feeds constantly, and pulling three feeds nightly without collapsing repeats means triple the lookups and triple the noise. Keying on ioc type and value, and keeping whichever copy has the higher confidence, means an indicator three feeds agree on survives with its strongest score — exactly the signal the next lesson needs to automate lookups against a SIEM.
